# Every word, in one place

**Generated** by `scripts/ip-narrative-review.py` from `apps/ip/content/*.json`. Do not edit this file - edit the JSON and regenerate, or the two will disagree and this one will lose.

This is the whole of the writing: every line the guide can say and every chain he can say it along. Nothing here is loaded by the app yet.

## What it is being judged against

A reviewer should know the rules before deciding a line is wrong, because several of these are counter-intuitive and were arrived at deliberately.

- **Evidence discipline, and four allowed classes of claim.** The instrument never claims to see what it has not asked about, so neither does he. Allowed: (1) what the instrument looked for and found or did not find, because it really did look; (2) disposition - what he likes, what steadies him; (3) the overwhelmingly likely reading of a record already on screen, phrased as inference; (4) hyperbole nobody could mistake for data. **Not allowed, and this was corrected after review: laundering an empirical claim through him.** "Most of what I have looked at" is not safe, because nothing records what he has looked at. Registered and observed are never conflated - absence of a route means not seen, not not-there.
- **The plate already states the fact.** A line that restates a number on screen is the wrong line. He is the only part of the product allowed to say what something *means*.
- **Three modes**, target 60 / 25 / 15 in the frequent tiers. `dry` is the default. `WRY` points at the internet and at him, **never at the thing the visitor just chose to go and look at**. `OPEN` has no joke and no undercut - if it relents into a joke it is not open, it is wry.
- **The unguarded mode must stay rare.** If he means it every time, meaning it is the formula and cannot be sincere. One-off lines are allowed to skew open: a line heard once can afford to mean something, a line heard forty times cannot.
- **Two readers at once** - somebody who has never heard the word *prefix*, and somebody who has run networks for thirty years, with the second never feeling patronised. Use the real word and cash it out at the thing on screen. Never simplify into something false. Banned outright: *did you know*, *simply*, *just*, *of course*, *obviously*, *basically*.
- **He is not teaching, he is pointing at his own work.** A surveyor says "that one has been empty since 1991". A curriculum says "did you know address space can remain unallocated".
- **`beautiful` may be used once in the entire product.** It is currently unused.

Full reasoning: `ip-guide-voice.md`, `ip-emotional-design.md`, `ip-two-audiences.md`, `ip-story-research.md`.

### `open.cold` — the first thing said, once the address is on screen

*fires once per visit · 4 lines*

> Highest-leverage writing in the product. Interesting, not moving - the emotional design forbids front-loading. FIRST MATCH WINS, most specific first, last entry is the fallback and must work for BOTH families. Registry-dependent branches are NOT here: the registry is deferred until the visitor moves and this fires before that, so they could never have run. They live in open.registry instead, which fires when the registry lands.

- dry *only addr-in-100.64/10* — You arrived on an address out of the carriers' own shared range. That is not supposed to reach this far.
- dry *only no-prefix* — Nothing I can see announces this exact range. Something larger around it is carrying you, which is ordinary and worth a look.
- dry *only v6* — An IPv6 address. You arrived in the larger of the two internets, and by some distance the emptier one.
- dry — That is the address this visit arrived on. Somebody is speaking for it. Let us go and find them.

# The chains

`at` is a fixed address, verified against the registry this app ships. `find` is a rule the sightline engine resolves at runtime, so the chain works without anyone having chosen the address in advance. `teaches` is never shown to anybody.

## Where you actually are

*`the-main-line` · main*

> Reconciles two lists that were never the same list: the seven beats in ip-plan-v2.md say what each step TEACHES, and the eight in ip-emotional-design.md say what each step FEELS. Teaching without a feeling is a curriculum; a feeling without a fact is a caption. Each beat below carries one of each, and the emotional beat is named so a later session cannot quietly drop it.

1. **`the visitor's own address`**
   > There. It exists somewhere other than here now, which is more than most of this map can say.
   
   <sub>teaches: it is a number, and somebody agreed to it</sub>
2. ***find:* the prefix the visitor's address is announced in**
   > Somebody stands up and says this range is theirs to speak for, and you are inside it. You have never met them.
   
   <sub>teaches: somebody speaks for you</sub>
3. ***find:* another prefix the same network announces**
   > Same network, different part of the map entirely. A network is not a place. It is a list of ranges somebody is willing to answer for.
   
   <sub>teaches: a network is not one range</sub>
4. ***find:* the whole of the visitor's address family**
   > All of it. Every number there will ever be in this family, and nearly all of them are taken. It still carried everything you did today.
   
   <sub>teaches: the size, and how little of it is left</sub>
5. ***find:* the whole of the visitor's address family**
   > All of it. Vastly more than has ever been handed out, and the part in use is a rounding error against the rest.
   
   <sub>teaches: the size, and how little of it has been needed</sub>
6. ***find:* the nearest root server**
   > Thirteen names hold up every name there is. And for years the register of which numbers had been given to whom was published, and largely kept, by one man.
   
   <sub>teaches: a handful of named things hold the rest up, and people looked after them by hand</sub>
7. ***find:* the origin network of any announced prefix**
   > A network can announce anything it likes. Every network decides for itself what to believe. Some of that is checked now - not all of it, and none of it was then.
   
   <sub>teaches: announcing is a claim, and every listener decides what to do with it</sub>
8. **`208.65.153.0`**
   > In 2008 a route meant to block one site inside one country escaped. For about two hours it pulled that site's traffic across the internet to somewhere it was never going. No one meant that to happen, which is the part worth sitting with.
   
   <sub>teaches: a claim meant for one country escaped</sub>
9. ***find:* the whole of the visitor's address family, again**
   > Every network decides for itself what to believe. And mostly, they agree.
   
   <sub>teaches: the same fact, read the other way</sub>

**Reveal —** No single authority tells any network which route to trust. Each one accepts, rejects or checks what it hears, and most of the time those decisions agree well enough to have carried everything you did today.

<sub>verified: 208.65.153.0 is present in space.bin as ARIN / US / 2006. The 2008 incident is sourced in docs/ip-story-research.md; RIPE's own analysis states it could not determine how many sites were affected, so the beat says traffic was pulled across the internet and does NOT claim universal failure. 'Some of that is checked now' is deliberately unquantified - origin validation is real, widely deployed and nowhere near universal, and any number would be wrong within a year.</sub>

## The boundary

*`the-boundary` · main · needs `the-main-line`*

> The plan's beats 6 and 7. The instrument turns around, and the product ends where it should. Fear appeal is the cheapest win available here and taking it would make this a worse product: show how little was kept and let the relief be the payoff.

1. ***find:* what actually crossed the wire to get here**
   > Everything I have shown you came from one number and a handful of public registers. Here is all of it.
   
   <sub>teaches: what a visit really reveals</sub>
2. ***find:* where our sight stops**
   > This is where I stop being able to see. Your address says where to send the answer. It does not say who you are, and I could not tell you.
   
   <sub>teaches: your address is not you</sub>

**Reveal —** An address is a delivery instruction that a great many strangers have agreed to honour. That is all it is, and it is not nothing.

## The oldest hands

*`oldest-hands` · side*

1. **`192.5.21.0`**
   > Nineteen eighty-two. There is nothing older in the register I carry.
   
   <sub>teaches: the record goes back further than people expect</sub>
2. **`12.0.0.0`**
   > Sixteen million addresses, to one organisation, in one go. The year after the oldest record there is.
   
   <sub>teaches: early allocations were enormous and casual</sub>
3. **`9.0.0.0`**
   > And again. They were not being careless. There was no reason yet to be careful.
   
   <sub>teaches: it kept happening for a decade</sub>

**Reveal —** For about ten years the internet was small enough that you could give away sixteen million addresses without anyone needing to think about it.

<sub>verified: 1982 is the earliest year present in space.bin. 12.0.0.0/8 is dated 1983 and is a whole /8. 9.0.0.0/8 is dated 1988.</sub>

## Set aside

*`never-usable` · side*

1. **`240.0.0.0`**
   > A sixteenth of the whole space, kept back for an addressing idea that never arrived. Nobody has ever been given any of it.
   
   <sub>teaches: space can be reserved and then never arrive</sub>
2. **`192.0.2.0`**
   > This one exists so that writing about addresses cannot accidentally name a real one.
   
   <sub>teaches: some addresses exist so that writing can be safe</sub>
3. **`2001:db8::`**
   > And the same again in IPv6, with room for every example anyone will ever need.
   
   <sub>teaches: the same idea, made much larger the second time</sub>

**Reveal —** Some of this space was never meant for the public internet. Kept back for an addressing idea, or handed to writing so examples cannot collide with anything real. Different reasons, same result: a place on the map that nobody is going to.

<sub>verified: All three are landmarks already in MARKS and are RFC facts, not lookups. On the date, which is contested: RFC 791 (1981-09) defined the class E range as reserved, while the IANA special-purpose registry records 1989-08 for its own entry. Those are two different events. The landmark line names 1981, which is the reservation rather than the registry record, and this chain names no date at all. Our own space.bin independently shows the range unallocated.</sub>

## The thirteen

*`the-thirteen` · side*

1. **`198.41.0.4`**

2. **`192.203.230.10`**

**Reveal —** Thirteen letters hold up every name on the internet, and the number is small enough that people argue about it.

<sub>verified: Root addresses come from the IANA root hints, already in MARKS, both families.</sub>

## Sold, and given back

*`sold-and-returned` · side · needs `oldest-hands`*

1. **`18.0.0.0`**
   > One of the big early ones. Look at who announces the halves of it now, and then look again.
   
   <sub>teaches: a founding-era /8, and what happened to it is visible rather than asserted</sub>
2. **`36.0.0.0`**
   > This one is registered on the other side of the world now, to a registry that did not exist when it was first handed out.
   
   <sub>teaches: the opposite decision, and the register records the consequence</sub>

**Reveal —** Once there was no more of it, address space became something you could transfer. Where a block is registered today and where it started are two different questions, and this map only answers the first.

<sub>verified: 36.0.0.0 reads APNIC / CN / 2011 in space.bin, which is consistent with the block having been returned and reissued. 18.0.0.0 reads ARIN / US / 1994. No holder is named by any line here; the plate names them from the live lookup.</sub>

## Small countries, old space

*`small-countries` · side*

1. ***find:* everything registered to Singapore**
   > Two thirds of this was handed out before 1993. Of every country holding more than a million addresses, none has a larger share that old.
   
   <sub>teaches: share of old space has nothing to do with size</sub>
2. ***find:* everything registered to North Korea**
   > One range. A thousand addresses, for a country.
   
   <sub>teaches: the other end of the same scale</sub>

**Reveal —** How much of this is registered to a country says almost nothing about how large the country is, and a great deal about how early the people asking for it got there.

<sub>verified: Computed from space.bin 2026-09-18: Singapore holds 27,894,080 v4 addresses of which 66.0% were allocated before 1993, the highest share of any country holding over a million. North Korea holds one range of 1,024 addresses.</sub>

## The quiet ones

*`the-quiet-ones` · side*

> Half authored, half computed - the template from docs/ip-story-research.md. The engine supplies the addresses because we cannot know them in advance; only the meaning is written.

1. ***find:* allocated before 2000, and nothing announces it**
   > Somebody was given this before the century turned. There is no route to it that I can see today.
   
   <sub>teaches: old and silent is a real and common state</sub>
2. ***find:* another, further away**
   > Another. They are not rare, once you know the shape of them.
   
   <sub>teaches: it is not a one-off</sub>
3. ***find:* the largest run of them nearby**
   > All of this is registered to somebody. None of it answers right now.
   
   <sub>teaches: the dark is not empty</sub>

**Reveal —** Allocated a long time ago, and no route to any of it that anyone here can see today. That is all this shows, and it is enough: the dark on this map is not empty space. It is held space that has gone quiet, and there is far more of it than anybody expects.

## Where the map is wrong

*`map-is-wrong` · side · needs `the-quiet-ones`*

> Gated for a real reason, not an arbitrary one: a block announced from the wrong continent is not STRANGE until you have watched an ordinary network's footprint stay where it was put. Entirely computed - it needs live routing data we do not ship.

1. ***find:* a prefix whose registered country differs from the country its origin network is registered under**
   > Registered under one country. Announced by a network registered under another. Neither of them is lying.
   
   <sub>teaches: the register records paperwork, not geography</sub>
2. ***find:* a second one, in a different registry**
   > Again, and nothing is wrong. This is what the two records are for.
   
   <sub>teaches: it is structural, not an error</sub>

**Reveal —** One record says which country the paperwork was filed under. The other says which network is announcing it. People read the first as a map of where the machines are, and it was never that - and this is two records disagreeing, not a measurement of anywhere.

# State of the writing

Derived from the content files on every regeneration, because the hand-written version of this section went stale the moment the main line was written and a reviewer found it before I did.

- **The spine exists.** *Where you actually are* and *The boundary*, 11 beats total.
- **9 chains, 29 beats**, of which **17 are `find` rules** the engine resolves at runtime rather than addresses anybody chose.
- **2 chains cannot ship yet:**
  - *The boundary* — Needs the inward half - phase H - which does not exist. The beats are written so the spine is settled and the side chains have something to point at, but nothing here can be built or locked yet.
  - *Sold, and given back* — The RETURN is not verified. space.bin shows 36.0.0.0 registered to CN under APNIC in 2011, which is consistent with a block having been given back and reissued and is not evidence that it was. Either a real historical source arrives or this chain does not ship. The beats are written so it can be decided rather than forgotten.
- **Still unwritten:** the celebration lines. Phase C machinery does not exist, and the rule for them is already set - he describes the play, like an announcer, and never congratulates the viewer.

# Known soft spots

- The unallocated bucket is **mostly about absence**, so its vocabulary clusters. Inherent to the subject, and the bucket most likely to read as bleak rather than dry.
- **The mode ratio counts lines, not hearings.** A tier that fires rarely contributes fewer heard lines than its share suggests, so these percentages are a proxy and a weighted one would be better.
- **Nothing varies by time, session length, or how full the notebook is.** Memory runs on one axis: unvisited, revisited, familiar.
- **A delivery scheduler is a hard requirement, not a nicety.** See `_delivery` in `guide.json`. There are 47 constantly-firing lines; speaking on every arrival would make this a talkative game.
